edges.relationship: Carter uses Cott’s history of marriage and nation to investigate how monogamous marriage was made into a contested foundation of Canadian national life.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008: 3–4 explicitly develops Cott’s Public Vows comparison and then states the Canadian extension; 67 uses the point that founding political orders establish marriage rules. Cott’s U.S. case is a resource, not identical Canadian evidence. The 2000 Harvard title and references are checked in Carter’s notes and bibliography; Cott’s original is not newly read. No formal mentorship or claim that every marriage followed this model.

edges.relationship: Carter adopts Perry’s Christian-conjugality formulation and uses her account of patriarchy and racial exclusion within the liberal order.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008: 4/note 7 identifies Perry’s specific formulation from her 2005 authored chapter in the Pickles/Rutherdale edited Contact Zones, page 115. Imperial Plots 8/notes 22–23 quotes Perry’s 2009 authored chapter in the Constant/Ducharme edited Liberalism and Hegemony, 275–276. This positive conceptual use coexists with Carter’s earlier appreciative criticism of Perry, edge_1613. No sole authorship of the edited volumes, full original chapter reading, or agreement with all Perry interpretations.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Van Kirk’s analysis of changing interracial marriage to explain hostility toward Indigenous women’s marriages within the later settler order.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008: 6 explicitly attributes the changing hostility to Van Kirk. Chapter 1 note 12 identifies the 2006 reprint of From Marrying-In to Marrying-Out in the Gleason/Perry edited Rethinking Canada, with Van Kirk’s 1980 Many Tender Ties and Perry’s 2001 book as further resources. This is a specified historical resource within Carter’s argument, not direct mentoring, sole credit for every fur-trade marriage claim, or independent verification of those originals. Existing group comparisons are not a Van Kirk→Carter personal claim.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Stoler’s account of colonial bourgeois formation to explain the policing of European marital dissent as well as colonized domestic life.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008:31/note 44 and 64/note 1 explicitly quote Stoler and apply the argument to interracial unions and other alternatives to monogamy. The cited authored chapter is Cultivating Bourgeois Bodies and Racial Selves in Catherine Hall’s edited Cultures of Empire (2000), 87–88 and 90. Hall’s editorial role is distinct; the original Stoler chapter is unread here. This bounded resource does not certify all Carter’s historical generalizations or convert her whole career into a single paradigm.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Burton’s account of unfinished colonial regulation to qualify the state’s power over Indigenous marriage and domestic life.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008:277 quotes and names Burton while concluding that colonial intervention disrupted without completely transforming Indigenous domestic law. Chapter 7 note 150 at 342 cites Gender, Sexuality and Colonial Modernities (1999), 1. The publisher contents identify Burton as editor and author of the introduction; this is not sole authorship of the collection. The underlying introduction and other chapters remain unread. The argument retains persistence and contestation alongside coercion, not a denial of colonial harm.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Brown’s warning about the custom-of-the-country label to distinguish diverse understandings and durations of fur-trade unions.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008:31 explicitly names Brown and uses her warning about implied uniformity before differentiating lifelong, lengthy but temporary and differently understood unions. Chapter 2 note 47 at 301 identifies Jennifer S. H. Brown’s Partial Truths: A Closer Look at Fur Trade Marriage (2002), 61, distinct from her 1980 book listed with Van Kirk in note 46. The original essay is unread; Carter also notes the scarcity of evidence about Indigenous wives’ perceptions. No assumption that a single marital custom governed all communities.

edges.relationship: Carter draws on Thompson’s interpretation of English wife-sale rituals to challenge the apparent timelessness of rigid marriage and divorce rules.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2008:65–67 explains and applies Thompson’s Customs in Common, cited in the 1993 New Press edition, 404–466, with specific quotations at 404, 406, 443 and 462. Thompson’s criticism of Hardy is reported through Carter, not freshly checked against either original. Carter expressly retains the inescapable property dimension while considering a negotiated public divorce mechanism. No independent validation of every example or generalized personal formation is claimed.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Wolfe’s logic-of-elimination framework when interpreting the dispossession and exclusion underlying prairie homesteading.
edges.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 6/note 6 explicitly names Wolfe and applies the formulation within her analysis of land, reserves and excluded Indigenous farmers. The note cites his 2006 Journal of Genocide Research article, 387; the bibliography supplies 387–409. The article remains unread in this dossier. This is a bounded resource in the 2016 book, read in its corrected 2018 reprint, not an influence inferred from citation alone or a retrospective classification of all Carter’s earlier work. Earlier edge_1315 retains its limits.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Philippa Levine’s gender-and-empire analysis to explain why profitable colonial masculinity excluded women and colonized people.
edges.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 7–8/notes 13, 20 explicitly frames the male imperial settler and quotes Levine’s particular exclusion argument. The bibliography identifies her authored Introduction: Why Gender and Empire? in her edited Gender and Empire (Oxford, 2004); notes cite 6–7. Authorship of this introduction is distinct from editing the collection and from Catherine Hall’s separate chapter. The original is unread here; this is a specific conceptual resource, not exclusive formation or a claim about Lawrence Levine.

edges.relationship: Carter uses Tosh alongside Levine to frame the gendered ideal of the white male settler as an imperial producer.
edges.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 7/note 13 jointly cites Levine’s introduction, 6, and Tosh’s Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005), 183–185, for this framing. This is a shared bibliographic and conceptual resource in her argument, not attribution of the quoted wording specifically to Tosh, sole intellectual origin, formal mentorship, or fresh reading of his book. The bibliography supplies the subtitle Essays on Gender, Family and Empire and Pearson/Longman publication.

edges.relationship: Greer criticizes Innis’s trade-centred conception of the colonial economy for obscuring household production and subsistence work.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1985:9 and 20–21 explicitly distinguishes Innis’s exchange focus from Pentland’s production relations, then argues that their colonial economy excludes much household output. Creighton is a joint target at 9. This is Greer’s specified methodological criticism, not independently verified output estimates, denial of every Innis contribution, or a fresh reading of Innis’s books. Existing group critique edge_1013 remains intact.

edges.relationship: Greer includes Creighton in his criticism of staples history for concentrating on exchange rather than social production.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1985:9 names Innis, Creighton and their contemporary followers together. The contrast credits Pentland’s attention to production relations while criticizing his trade-centred categories. It is not a wholesale assessment of Creighton’s career or a fresh reading of The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence. The later household-production discussion supports the scope, without assigning every later sentence specifically to Creighton.

edges.relationship: Greer uses Marx’s reading of Wakefield to distinguish capitalist dispossession from the claim that colonial land policy alone could remake society.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1985:21/note 22 expressly approves Marx’s use of Wakefield as a revealing bourgeois admission rather than a practicable programme. The reference is Capital, Moscow 1954, volume 1, chapter 33; its edition/translation and original chapter are not newly read. This particular argumentative resource is distinct from generic Marxist identity. Earlier 10 contrasts Marx/Engels’s broad class relations with Pentland’s ladder of stages and retains their joint conceptual credit.

edges.relationship: Greer uses Van Kirk’s history of women in the fur trade to expose the gender bias of equating labour with salaried male work.
edges.evidence_note: Own 1985:20 explicitly credits Van Kirk before arguing that a focus on wage labour writes productive women out of the household economy. Note 19 cites Many Tender Ties, Winnipeg 1980. This is a specific historical resource for his critique, not mentorship or a new reading of Van Kirk’s original. Greer’s claims about aggregate subsistence output remain his unreplicated argument.

edges.relationship: Greer uses Benton’s account of maritime and uneven sovereignty to distinguish early modern empire from territorial colonization.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2018:5–6 explicitly credits Benton and others, citing A Search for Sovereignty (2010) in notes 13–14 and 16. Subrahmanyam, Bertrand, Stoler and Maier retain their separate supporting roles; Benton is not sole origin. This conceptual use supports his correction of Said’s land-centred formulation. The original Benton book and other cited works remain unread here.

edges.relationship: Greer challenges Cronon’s description of colonial land as capital when arguing for the limited role of capitalism in early North American property formation.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2018:3/note 6 quotes Changes in the Land (1983),77, as an influential example, then 3–4 stresses residence, subsistence and settler commons. This is a particular periodization/interpretation objection, not rejection of Cronon’s whole ecological history or independent reading of the original book. Dispossession and exploitation are retained rather than made benign.

edges.relationship: Greer qualifies Said’s land-possession definition of empire, arguing that it better describes colonization than early modern imperial reach.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2018:5–6 quotes Culture and Imperialism, cited in the 1994 Knopf manifestation,78, and proposes replacing empire with colonization in that formulation. Benton’s maritime and nodal account is a positive resource. This is a narrow early modern conceptual correction, not a wholesale dismissal of Said or a newly read original. Spanish conquest and uneven American territorial control remain differentiated.

edges.relationship: Greer adapts Arendt’s property–wealth distinction to explain how household-based colonial property could be expansive and dispossessing without being chiefly profit-driven.
edges.evidence_note: Own publisher HTML, section Property Formation in Comparative Perspective, explicitly uses and modifies Arendt’s distinction. Note 50 identifies The Human Condition (Chicago 1958) and the named private-realm/property and property/wealth sections; the original is unread and its organization is not independently collated. Greer differs from Arendt’s postwar diagnosis and expressly refuses a benign or egalitarian reading of settler households. No printed paragraph page is invented from unpaginated HTML.

edges.relationship: Greer adopts Wolfe’s critique of naturalized settler history and continuing dispossession while seeking a more differentiated colonial chronology.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2019:62–63 explicitly calls for taking on board Wolfe’s historiographical critique, developed further by Veracini, and values the structure-not-event formulation. Notes 2–3 and 7–8 distinguish Wolfe 2007,1999,2006 and Veracini 2010; originals remain unread here. Positive uptake coexists with Greer’s scope objection; neither automatic full agreement nor a direct personal teaching relationship is inferred.

edges.relationship: Greer argues that Wolfe’s settlement–exploitation dyad needs extension to capture other overlapping colonial forms in northern North America.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2019:63–64 names Wolfe’s Australia/India focus, then introduces imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism as additional modes. Greer insists these coexist and overlap rather than form self-contained stages. He expressly values Wolfe’s critique and does not attribute every casual temporal flattening to Wolfe himself. Existing group critique edge_1012 remains; original Wolfe texts are unread.

edges.relationship: Palmer criticizes the coherence of Greer and Radforth’s Colonial Leviathan while valuing its articles and reinterpretation of responsible government.
edges.evidence_note: Complete signed review 365–367, especially 366, distinguishes this collection-level objection from his separate criticism of Bruce Curtis. Greer and Ian Radforth are joint editors, not sole authors of all chapters. Palmer credits the volume’s revision of responsible government and calls for broader synthesis; neither total dismissal nor a new reading of the 1992 collection is claimed. Existing group comparison edge_1011 keeps its original qualifications.

sources.title: Publisher identity for Antoinette Burton’s edited Gender, Sexuality and Colonial Modernities
sources.citation: Routledge, Gender, Sexuality and Colonial Modernities, copyright 1999; edited by Antoinette Burton; contents identify her authored introduction.

verification.note: Retained official indexed publisher metadata identifies editor, 1999 copyright and introduction author. The current direct publisher request returned 403; no full introduction or collection reading is claimed. Metadata corroborates the attribution in Carter’s chapter 7 note 150, rather than substituting for Carter’s substantive use.

screq_carter_2008.note: Additional selected primary reading from the actual AU Press open publisher PDF: opening passages 3–6 and 8–17, selected acknowledgments xi–xii, 31, 64–67 and 277, plus their exact notes and bibliography. Cott, Perry, Van Kirk, Stoler, Brown, Thompson and Burton retain distinct work-specific roles. Chapter 7 note 150 concerns Burton’s edited collection and authored introduction. Stoler locators are 31 and 64, not 16. Thompson’s customary-divorce argument retains the property qualification; Brown’s warning preserves varied unions and scarce Indigenous wives’ testimony. Earlier 3–9 reading remains intact. No whole 399-page PDF/book or cited original work reading, legal validation or universal Indigenous marriage model is claimed.

p4b_carter_2016.note: Additional selected 3–9 passages and corresponding notes/bibliography read in the actual Manitoba publisher PDF, corrected 2018 reprint of 2016 book. Earlier selected 3–11/19–23 record is preserved, not silently extended to whole book reading. Explicit Wolfe formulation 6/note 6, Levine and shared Tosh framing 7–8/notes 13, 20, and Perry liberal-order quotations 8/notes 22–23 have specified argumentative uses. Settler women’s exclusion and participation in dispossession remain jointly qualified; historical quotes are objects of Carter’s analysis, not the atlas’s voice. General acknowledgment and editorial roles do not automatically establish formation. Original cited works remain unread.

df01_ahenakew_medicine2003.note: Reread the complete signed Medicine review 196–197 in publisher PDF leaves 2–3, beginning after the preceding Alfred Fisher review. Harold Cardinal, Paul Chartrand, Ahenakew and Dickason are Medicine-attributed scholarly resources. Her quoted Christine Welsh discussion and Big Bear example are distinct; no relay of those claims to Ahenakew or Dickason. Existing edges 1701/1715 remain, with Carter’s 1999 survey and underlying originals unread.

df02_dickason_carter2001_review.note: Retained original repository review text confirms Dickason’s corrective-history praise and idealization/equality criticism already represented by edge 1712. No fresh facsimile or 1999 book reading is claimed; the original review page 235 and sole reviewer remain distinct from the repository’s metadata. Her reception and Medicine’s reported Dickason resource coexist.

lof_greer_2018.note: Fresh actual Cambridge ten-page excerpt 1–10 read, with its notes; full frontmatter title/imprint and acknowledgmentsxv–xvii read. Public publisher HTML additionally supplies the complete Property Formation in Comparative Perspective section and note 50, including the Arendt distinction. This does not claim a new complete 1–24 reading; the earlier whole-introduction record is preserved. Cronon and Said objections, Benton’s resource and Arendt’s modification remain work-specific. Chantal Cramaussel’s substantive corrective intervention, Neal Salisbury’s whole-manuscript reading and Kate Desbarats’s critical contribution are important missing-endpoint holds; generic helper lists are not automatically formation. Epigraphs, editorial roles, chapter/reprint and original-unread limits remain distinct.

pe139_greer_pentland_1985.note: Fresh original journal 18-page PDF retrieved; selected 7–11 and 18–22 read, preserving the earlier complete 7–22 record without a second whole-body claim. Innis/Creighton exchange categories, Marx/Engels conceptual distinctions and specific Marx/Wakefield use, and Van Kirk’s women’s-labour resource retain exact roles. Pentland is the central missing endpoint, not substituted by his interpreters. Bibliographic OCR is checked against context and key images where needed; original Pentland/Innis/Creighton/Marx/Van Kirk works remain unread. Historical and numerical claims are Greer’s and not independently replicated.

screq_greer_2019_jcha.note: Fresh original Érudit 27-leaf PDF includes cover plus printed 61–86. Selected 61–64 and corresponding notes 80–81 reread; earlier complete 61–86 scope remains distinct. Greer values Wolfe and Veracini while extending the dyad, and explicitly proposes coexisting overlapping modes rather than chronological stages. Woolford/Benvenuto and Richter supply other critiques, not every one assigned to Wolfe. Named citation clusters and originals are not automatic personal formation. The article derives from a keynote; no full WMQ 2019 or original Wolfe reading is newly claimed.

pe139_curtis_palmer_1993.note: Fresh original journal 72-page reviews PDF retrieved. Only complete signed Palmer 365–367, PDF leaves 3–5, reread; adjacent Jack Tar review is excluded. Curtis criticism and Greer/Radforth collection coherence are distinct, with responsible-government praise and qualified call for synthesis preserved. Individual contributors and joint editors retain their roles. No whole collection or Curtis book reading is claimed. Earlier dedicated Curtis reading scope remains intact.

rationale: Existing endpoints only; preserve named mediation, coauthorship, critical qualifications, edition and reading limits. All old graph records unchanged apart from append-only source reading notes. Tocqueville excluded as an owned dossier or newly read primary body, not as an existing resource endpoint in another historian’s own testimony. No new biographies, fields, life facts, chronology or dissertation analysis. OpenAlex remains paused.
